transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Time: 15:00 EDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM - partial), Asha Patel (Verdigris Head of AI), Tom Reynolds (Verdigris CISO), Claire Wu (Verdigris Eng Mgr), Marcus Li (Verdigris Platform)

Summary:
A discovery focused on which hosting model (Hosted API vs Dedicated reserved pools vs Private VPC/on-prem) meets Verdigris Bancorp's compliance and log-retention constraints (GDPR + financial services audit requirements + internal e-discovery). Primary concerns: full control of logs, key residency (KMS), ability to redact or drop PII from logs, retention windows, evidence for auditors, and network isolation. Customer leaning toward Redwood Dedicated or Private but needs clarity on how much evidence Redwood can provide and what controls remain with Verdigris.

Topics:
- Current stack and where inference calls originate
- Log collection, redaction, and retention policies
- Key management and key residency requirements (KMS/HSM)
- SSO/SAML and RBAC for developer access
- Legal/Compliance evidence (SOC2, runbooks, exportable logs)
- Pilot/POC plan and timeline

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I'm Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE; with me is Luis Ortega, our solutions engineer. We'll run through hosting options and dig into your compliance constraints.
[00:12] Asha Patel: Hi, thanks, Maya. Yes, we wanted to map hosting options specifically how logs are held and what we can show auditors.
[00:18] Tom Reynolds: Hi, Tom here - CISO. Short context: Verdigris handles payment servicing and custodial accounts so anything that touches customer data is, like, under heavy regulatory scope. We're evaluating if Redwood Hosted is viable or if we need Dedicated or Private.
[00:30] Luis Ortega: Got it. Quick run: can you share how your inference traffic currently flows? Are calls from client apps, backend servers, or an internal ML infra?
[00:40] Claire Wu: Most call paths originate from backend microservices in our VPC, then outbound to external APIs. We could proxy through a dedicated outbound gateway if needed.
[00:50] Marcus Li: We use AWS in us-east-1 primarily. We have an internal KMS for keys and strict egress controls.
[01:00] Maya Chen: Helpful. A few things we'll want to sync on: where keys live, exact retention windows, and whether you need key escrow or on-prem HSM. Also, whether you require survey-grade proof for auditors like signed attestations or raw log exports.
[01:12] Tom Reynolds: We need both: signed evidence for SOC2-like reviewers and raw-ish event logs for internal forensic teams. Also, logs must be retained for a minimum of seven years for certain product lines — it's, um, long.
[01:25] Luis Ortega: Okay, so a couple tradeoffs: Hosted can be the fastest to stand up but we can't offer KMS keys that are customer-managed in the Hosted control plane; we can, however, offer dedicated encryption-at-rest per-customer and limited audit artifacts. For Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and stronger isolation; Private gives you the strongest control including bringing-your-own-KMS and full control of logs.
[01:44] Asha Patel: When you say "limited audit artifacts" for Hosted, what is actually not available?
[01:48] Luis Ortega: In Hosted, we retain ingress/request metadata for routing and billing; we can provide per-request metadata (timestamps, model used, latency) and aggregated token usage. But we generally do not provide raw request payloads or full output text in exported logs for Hosted tenants unless we have a contractual data retention agreement and encryption separation — and even then, it's limited.
[02:05] Claire Wu: So we can't get raw prompts back from Hosted, unless we enter a special arrangement?
[02:10] Luis Ortega: Correct, for privacy and multi-tenant safety we avoid exporting raw content by default. If you need raw content for forensic audit, Private (or Private on VPC) is the recommended path.
[02:18] Tom Reynolds: Hmm. Our legal team will push back if we can't get event-level logs for certain high-risk workflows. We also have an internal policy for key control — keys must be in our HSM or under our KMS control.
[02:30] Maya Chen: Noted. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own) and HSM-level controls — we can build an integration with your KMS provider and optionally a key-escrow workflow. We'll document that in the diagram.
[02:42] Marcus Li: For Dedicated — do you support VPC peering or private link style connections? We can't have outbound connections to public endpoints for production traffic.
[02:50] Luis Ortega: Dedicated supports private connectivity. We commonly use AWS PrivateLink or transit VPC connections. For Private installs (VPC-delivered or on-prem), we run a control plane that can be partially customer-managed and a data plane that lives in your VPC, so traffic never leaves your network.
[03:05] Asha Patel: What's the story on log redaction? We need PII redaction inline before anything is stored.
[03:12] Luis Ortega: There are multiple layers: client-side redaction (recommended), in-flight filters before logs hit storage, and post-processing redaction. On Private deployments you can configure the in-flight filter rules and which fields are hashed or dropped. On Dedicated we can enable configurable redaction pipelines but because the control plane still touches some metadata, you need contractual assurances.
[03:28] Tom Reynolds: Can those filters run deterministically so our auditors can validate them?
[03:32] Luis Ortega: Yes, we can produce rule sets and hashes that auditors can validate. We also support proof-of-redaction logs — e.g., we can show a record that indicates data matched a redaction rule without showing the raw value.
[03:45] Claire Wu: About retention: we have product lines that require 7 years, others 3 to 5. Does Redwood allow per-route retention policies?
[03:54] Maya Chen: Yes, on Private deployments we support per-model or per-route retention policies; on Dedicated it's configurable but more limited and likely per-tenant. Hosted is mostly platform-standard retention unless you negotiate retention add-ons.
[04:08] Asha Patel: Another requirement: SSO via SAML, role mapping to RBAC with separation of duties. Devs shouldn't be able to pull logs without approvals.
[04:17] Luis Ortega: We integrate with SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and can map groups to roles. For Private you manage the IdP directly; for Hosted we federate and issue tokens with scoped RBAC. We can lock down logging access to specific roles.
[04:30] Tom Reynolds: What about audit trails for operator actions — like who rotated keys, who changed retention policies?
[04:36] Maya Chen: We provide operator audit logs across all hosting modes. On Hosted, operator logs are available as redacted audit trails; on Dedicated/Private you can have full operator logs forwarded to your SIEM (e.g., Splunk, S3 bucket) via secure forwarding.
[04:50] Marcus Li: Are there examples of financial customers who've done the full Private install on-prem? We'd like referenceability for our compliance board.
[04:57] Luis Ortega: Yes, we've done several banks and custody platforms in Private mode. I'll put anonymized case references in the follow-up and include architecture diagrams.
[05:07] Asha Patel: Timeline question: our internal procurement is two-phase — initial POC for 6 weeks, then production. We need to know how long each hosting mode takes to stand up.
[05:18] Maya Chen: Typical times: Hosted is minutes to hours; Dedicated can be low weeks (2–4) depending on capacity and contract; Private VPC deliveries are 4–8 weeks depending on network and compliance scoping; on-prem can be longer, usually 8–12+ weeks for packaged installs and audits.
[05:33] Claire Wu: Costs: can you give very rough delta between Dedicated and Private?
[05:36] Luis Ortega: Very rough: Dedicated has committed monthly pricing tied to GPU pools — you're paying for reserved capacity plus management; Private typically adds a platform fee and higher deployment/configuration costs. We'll share a ballpark in follow-up — exacts depend on model families, qps, and retention obligations.
[05:49] Tom Reynolds: One more — data residency: we need EU data to stay within EU zones for certain customers, and US data in US. Can Redwood guarantee regional locking?
[05:58] Maya Chen: Hosted offers region-specific clusters and we can pin workloads to regions; Dedicated can be placed in region-specific capacity; Private by design keeps everything in your VPC region. We'll need to map the flow and ensure backups and logs are also region-locked.
[06:12] Asha Patel: Ok, practical question: for the POC we can use Hosted but with strict redaction and pseudo-data — would that satisfy initial eval?
[06:21] Maya Chen: Yes, many customers do a Hosted proof-of-concept with synthetic or redacted data to validate latency, integration, and tooling. Then they move to Dedicated or Private for production if compliance requires it.
[06:30] Marcus Li: Regarding encryption — at-rest and in-transit are table stakes, but we need to confirm key lifecycle management is auditable. Can Redwood provide rotation logs and attestations?
[06:40] Luis Ortega: We can provide rotation logs and KMS audit exports when using customer-managed KMS. For Hosted with Redwood-managed keys, we provide rotation reports but not the underlying key material. For Private, you own the keys and we produce the runbooks and logging hooks.
[06:55] Tom Reynolds: On the question of legal holds — if we have to freeze logs for litigation, can you support legal hold requests and export workflows?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Yes. For Private we fully support legal hold workflows and exportable archives. For Dedicated/Hosted, we support export of available artifacts but the capabilities vary — we will document exact artifact types per mode.
[07:16] Claire Wu: We're also worried about developer access. Could a developer inadvertently pull whole datasets into a prompt?
[07:22] Luis Ortega: This is where prefix caching and client-side filters come in. We recommend policy-based prompts and instrumentation to catch large dumps. Also RBAC and approved prompt templates.
[07:34] Asha Patel: Do you have a pattern for demonstrable redaction that auditors accept? We need something that will pass our internal audit.
[07:40] Luis Ortega: Yes, we often deliver a combination: 1) deterministic redaction rules (regexp/hash), 2) proof-of-redaction logs (hash-only record of match), and 3) attestations + runbooks. We'll share a reference artifact.
[07:52] Marcus Li: Are there SLA differences between Dedicated and Private?
[07:56] Maya Chen: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; Private SLAs can be negotiated — since production responsibilities are more shared in Private, SLA specifics are part of the enterprise contract.
[08:06] Tom Reynolds: Can we get a sample contract clause around data residency and deletion?
[08:10] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll draft sample language for data residency, deletion timelines, and breach notification commitments.
[08:16] Jordan Lee (CSM): Quick note — we also have tooling for cost telemetry and token-level breakdowns if you want to tie spending to models and routes.
[08:24] Claire Wu: That will help. Our finance folks will want to see cost trending in the POC.
[08:28] Asha Patel: For the POC scope we want three things: 1) latency/throughput benchmarks for our workload, 2) integration test with SAML SSO, 3) validate redaction pipeline with synthetic PII. Is that doable?
[08:39] Luis Ortega: Yes, that's a common POC. We can run benchmarks on Hosted then replicate on Dedicated for delta measurement. For SAML and redaction we'll need a short integration window.
[08:48] Maya Chen: I'll propose a timeline in follow-up: week 0 onboarding, week 1 SAML + network, week 2 redaction tests and small benchmark, week 3 deeper load test, week 4 wrap and results.
[08:58] Tom Reynolds: How about logs forwarding — do you support pushing logs to our corp S3 with server-side encryption and restricted IAM roles?
[09:04] Luis Ortega: Yes, we can forward logs to S3 with SSE-KMS and role-restricted write-only credentials. For Private, you'll own the bucket; for Dedicated we can write to a customer-managed bucket or provide a secure buffer.
[09:18] Claire Wu: Any blockers we should flag now?
[09:20] Maya Chen: The two potential blockers are: 1) key residency if you absolutely must hold keys on-prem without any cloud-managed KMS, and 2) long retention windows combined with retention of raw content — that typically pushes to Private. If you can accept pseudonymized/sanitized logs for Hosted, you can do more in Hosted.
[09:36] Asha Patel: I think legal will push for Private if they see we need 7-year raw retention. But for product teams a Hosted POC with synthetic data will be acceptable.
[09:45] Marcus Li: Marcus: can we get an example redaction rule set and a sample proof-of-redaction artifact?
[09:50] Luis Ortega: Yep, will include that in follow-up.
[09:54] -- brief crosstalk while someone switches screens --
[10:12] Claire Wu: Slight tangent — do you support model quantization or custom models in Private? We might want to host a smaller quantized model for cost reasons.
[10:20] Luis Ortega: Yes, Private supports custom model variants and we support recommended quantization profiles. Dedicated can support certain quantized model families as well — depends on compatibility. We'll advise on throughput tradeoffs.
[10:30] Asha Patel: Competitors — we're also speaking with Anthropic and evaluating an internal self-host option. Cost/perf and compliance will drive us.
[10:38] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll make sure to show clear SLOs and audit artifacts in the follow-up to compare apples-to-apples.
[10:46] Tom Reynolds: Ok, last operational question: incident response. If there's a compromise, what is Redwood's process and notification SLA?
[10:53] Maya Chen: We have incident response runbooks, 24/7 pager for severity 1s for enterprise customers with escalation to our executive team. Breach notification timelines are contract-specific but our standard is 72 hours for confirmed incidents; we'll include those commitments in the sample contract language.
[11:07] Marcus Li: Good.
[11:10] Maya Chen: Alright, let's capture next steps and action items.

Action items (read back):
- Maya Chen to send SOC2 report, ISO docs, sample contract clauses around data residency and deletion, and reference customer notes (anonymized) by 2026-07-12.
- Luis Ortega to share Private deployment network diagram (S3 forwarding, VPC endpoints, NACL examples) and sample redaction rule set by 2026-07-14.
- Claire Wu / Verdigris to provide their log retention policy and legal contact for escalation by 2026-07-16.
- Team to schedule POC kickoff for week of 2026-07-20 (tentative) pending legal sign-off.

Questions asked during call:
- Can Hosted provide raw request/response logs? (Answer: Not by default; special contractual arrangements only.)
- Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM? (Answer: Yes — Private supports BYO KMS/HSM; Dedicated can for some cases.)
- Can logs be forwarded to customer S3 with SSE-KMS? (Answer: Yes, supported.)

Links & artifacts referenced:
- "Redwood Private deployment guide (draft)" — link shared in chat (will be included in follow-up).
- Sample redaction rule set (placeholder link).
- SOC2 + ISO attestations (to be sent).

Wrap / Recap [11:30]:
Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Recap — Hosted POC with synthetic data is OK for benching and integrations; production with long raw retention and customer-managed keys likely requires Private. We'll send the docs and schedule POC kickoff week of July 20.
Asha Patel: Thanks, that sounds good. We'll align legal and come back with definitive decision.
Tom Reynolds: Appreciate the thorough answers. Expect legal to reach out.

End meeting.
